full: Ultimate Cron to master all automated tasks in Drupal Drupal Cron Publicado 27/08/2024 Lectura de 12 minutos Representation of Drupal's cron task manager as Salvador Dalí's “The Persistence of Memory” Representation of Drupal's cron task manager as Salvador Dalí's “The Persistence of Memory” Representation of Drupal's cron task manager as Salvador Dalí's “ The Persistence of Memory ” In Drupal , managing automated tasks is crucial, but the built-in cron can be limiting. Ultimate Cron offers a flexible solution that allows you to customize the frequency and scheduling of each task, thus optimizing site performance and preventing server overload. In this article, I show how to start making the most of this module and use it efficiently and effectively. The Drupal core includes its own integrated cron that allows you to schedule automated tasks, which provides the ability to add custom tasks that will run when cron is triggered in Drupal . The issue is that Drupal executes all tasks during cron execution, which can be inconvenient if you need one of them to run more or less frequently. This poses the dilemma of whether to run cron tasks less frequently, thus having a smaller impact on the server and leaving behind tasks that need to be run more often; or, on the other hand, to run tasks more frequently, thus overloading the server with less necessary tasks. It is also possible that a daily task that requires significant execution time, higher server power, or the server's full bandwidth should run during periods of low user activity (e.g., at night, unless it's a programming forum server 🌚).     The ultimate cron. To address this issue, there is a contributed project in Drupal called Ultimate Cron , which allows you to configure and schedule cron tasks individually. To install it, do so like any other module in Drupal with Composer by running the following command in the console: composer require drupal/ultimate_cron And enable it from the “ Extend ” administration section or via Drush in the console with the command: drush en ultimate_cron After enabling it, all cron tasks will appear at /admin/config/system/cron/jobs or Administration > Configuration > System > Cron > Cron Jobs : Drupal "Ultimate Cron" jobs Drupal "Ultimate Cron" jobs   You can now sort tasks, edit them, disable them, or view the reports they generate during execution. When editing a task from “ Operations ,” you can configure the scheduler to be Simple (Executes the task every 1 minute, 5 minutes, 15 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours, 6 hours, 12 hours, once a day, or once a week) or to be of type Crontab , which is a way to configure natural time periods programmatically (e.g., every Wednesday at 12:00 PM). Don’t worry if you don’t fully understand Crontab , there is a small help section on the same page that guides its use, and if not, you can use Crontab Guru . Additionally, you can configure execution times and reports, but my recommendation is to leave it as is by default unless you need something specific.     Creating a new cron task. What’s interesting about Ultimate Cron is the ability to configure custom tasks since generally, tasks from other contributed modules tend to be quite uniform. If the task, like those from contributed modules, is also quick and painless for the system, the best and fastest implementation is a hook_cron() in a custom module with the code you want to execute in the cron task: /** * Implements hook_cron(). */ function example_cron() { \Drupal::logger("example")->notice("Hey there, I’m using WhatsApp, I mean, Drupal."); } And now, for Ultimate Cron to detect the new cron task, you need to discover it using the “ Discover Tasks ” button at /admin/config/system/cron/jobs . And congratulations, you’ve created your first configurable Drupal cron task. Remember that, as with all configurations in Drupal , you must export it to consolidate it . Drupal "Ultimate Cron" example job Drupal "Ultimate Cron" example job       Problems, problems, and more problems. Implementing a cron task in a hook is great, but what if you want to create more than one cron task per module? Surely someone has created many custom modules just for this purpose. We don’t judge anyone here, but there’s a better solution: install cron configurations. For this, the easiest approach is to use the YML configuration file of another cron as a template, for example, the configuration file of the example task created earlier ( ultimate_cron.job.example_cron.yml ): uuid: 95f9d95c-3fb0-4a36-a20f-223b496272za langcode: en status: true dependencies: module: - example title: 'Default cron handler' id: example_cron weight: 0 module: example callback: example_cron scheduler: id: simple launcher: id: serial logger: id: database Starting from the content of this file, copy its contents to your custom module inside config/cron/ultimate_cron.job.example_cron_two.yml and remove the uuid line (the first line), langcode , and weight , as these will be configured by the system. Also, change the id to some identifier representing the cron task, for example example_cron_two , and the title to something similar to the identifier, such as “ Example cron 2 ” (Extremely descriptive, I know). Now, importantly, callback will be the response function of the cron task where its logic will be implemented. It’s best to give it a name that does not interfere with other functions, such as “ _example_two_cron_job_ ”, and module is the module where the response function will be implemented (so it can be called primarily, acting as a dependency). After these adjustments, the file config/cron/ultimate_cron.job.example_cron_two.yml should look like this: status: true dependencies: module: - example title: 'Example cron 2' id: example_cron_two module: example callback: _example_two_cron_job_ scheduler: id: simple launcher: id: serial logger: id: database And you should define the response function within the custom module: /** * Execute example_cron_two cron task. */ function _example_two_cron_job_() { \Drupal::logger("example")->notice("Hey there, I’m using WhatsApp, I mean, Drupal (Again)"); } This process can be repeated as many times as needed for cron tasks in a module, and finally, import all configurations with the command: drush config-import --source=modules/custom/example/config/cron --partial -y Configure them for scheduling, and export the configuration to consolidate it along with the rest of the settings.     Conclusion. Properly managing cron tasks in Drupal is essential for optimizing system performance and ensuring that necessary processes run at the right time. The contributed module Ultimate Cron proves to be an effective solution, allowing detailed and customized configuration of each scheduled task. This not only prevents server overload but also ensures that each task runs with the ideal frequency. With Ultimate Cron , managing cron tasks in Drupal becomes a controlled and efficient process, enhancing both server performance and site functionality.   /es/articulos/ultimate-cron-para-dominar-todas-las-tareas-automaticas-en-drupal /en/articles/ultimate-cron-master-all-automated-tasks-drupal

full: Visual Studio Code extensions for PHP and Drupal development Visual Studio Code Extensions Drupal PHP Publicado 01/05/2024 Lectura de 13 minutos Visual Studio Code logo Visual Studio Code logo Visual Studio Code logo - Wikipedia Visual Studio Code extensions that have transformed the development experience in PHP and Drupal . From syntax highlighting to intelligent code completion, these essential tools streamline workflow and ensure more efficient, error-free coding. As I continue to complete developments and diversify the technologies I work with, I realize that the extensions I have installed in Visual Studio Code proliferate to optimize my time in one way or another. I don't even remember the first time I installed Microsoft's code editor, but the main advantage I saw then was its price: free, and since then I haven't used another because I'm already used to Visual Studio Code . I have to admit that at the beginning of my career I was unaware of the existence of the editor's extensions (which also have the advantage in their price as most of them are free, at least for installing them), but after some experience in PHP and Drupal , I would like to share in no particular order a small list of Visual Studio Code extensions that are key in development with these technologies.     Drupal by Stanislav Romanov   Drupal by Stanislav Romanov The Drupal extension offers a comprehensive set of tools for development in this popular CMS. It facilitates programming in Drupal projects, providing syntax highlighting, hook completion, Twig and services completion, as well as global variables, complying with Drupal's programming standards through phpcs and phpcbf . It also offers the ability to search the Drupal API documentation, autocomplete translations in PHP , Twig , and JavaScript files, validation and autocompletion for YAML files, and analysis with PHPStan , although this last functionality is experimental. This tool is essential for Drupal developers looking to improve their workflow in Visual Studio Code, ensuring more efficient development with fewer errors.   Drupal Smart Snippets by Andy Blum   Drupal Smart Snippets by Andy Blum The extension provides comprehensive support for Drupal development, offering contextual code snippets and intelligent features to streamline the coding process. These snippets are built from the core of Drupal , encompassing both hooks and form and render elements. The extension is a successor to Drupal 8 Snippets and employs advanced techniques such as automatic hook and element replacement based on the current file's name, as well as automatic generation of additional properties for form elements from documentation. Additionally, smart snippets for services allow easy access to core Drupal services with IntelliSense suggestions. Installation is straightforward through the Visual Studio Code extensions menu, and the extension is regularly updated to ensure compatibility with the latest Drupal versions. This extension significantly enhances the productivity of Drupal developers by providing a more efficient and precise coding experience in Visual Studio Code .   PHP Intelephense by Ben Mewburn   PHP Intelephense by Ben Mewburn    (Official Extension) The PHP Intelephense extension offers powerful code processing for PHP development, with a range of essential features that enhance productivity. It provides rapid code completion for symbols and keywords both in the current document and throughout the workspace, with automatic inclusion of use statements. Additionally, it offers detailed signature help for constructors, methods, and functions, as well as support for quickly navigating to definition and finding all references within the workspace. It also provides advanced static analysis with multiple diagnostics for open files, PSR-12 compatible formatting, built-in intelligence for HTML , JavaScript , and CSS , and highlighting of references and keywords. The extension also features an advanced PHPDoc type system, support for PHPStorm metadata, and additional functions such as symbol renaming and code folding. Some premium features are available for purchase, such as automatic PHPDoc generation, smart syntax tree tracking, and useful code actions. In summary, the extension is an essential tool for PHP developers looking to enhance their workflow in Visual Studio Code .   Twig Language 2 by mblode   Twig Language 2 by mblode The Twig Language 2 extension provides comprehensive support for Twig templating in Visual Studio Code , enhancing the coding experience for Drupal developers and other users working with Twig . It offers syntax highlighting for Twig code embedded in HTML , CSS , JavaScript , and other languages, with intelligent code completion and suggestions for Twig tags, filters, and functions. Additionally, it provides detailed syntax validation and error checking, with support for advanced Twig constructs such as macros and blocks. The extension also offers useful features such as customizable snippets, bracket matching, and automatic indentation. Installation is straightforward through the Visual Studio Code extensions menu, and the extension is regularly updated to ensure compatibility with the latest Twig and Visual Studio Code versions. Overall, the extension significantly improves the Twig templating workflow in Visual Studio Code , making it an essential tool for Drupal developers and other users working with Twig .   YAML by Red Hat   YAML by Red Hat    (Official Extension) This extension provides robust support for the YAML language, including built-in support for Kubernetes syntax. It offers several useful features such as YAML validation, document outline schema, autocompletion, hover information support over a node, and code formatting. The extension also allows associating JSON schemas to YAML files to enhance validation and coding experience. This extension is particularly useful for developers working with YAML files, especially in Kubernetes environments.   Drupal Syntax Highlighting by Marco Stazi   Drupal Syntax Highlighting by Marco Stazi The Drupal Syntax Highlighting extension provides syntax highlighting support for specific Drupal file types such as .module , .inc , .theme , etc. This extension simplifies the process of setting up syntax highlighting rules for Drupal files by providing a ready-to-use solution. Instead of manually adding file types to your settings.json file. This extension is useful for Drupal developers who want their code to be highlighted and formatted correctly within Visual Studio Code . It supports various Drupal file extensions, including .module , .inc , .theme , .install , .make , .profile , .test , and .info .   DDEV Manager by Biati Digital   DDEV Manager by Biati Digital    (Official Extension) This extension simplifies DDEV project management by providing a centralized and easy-to-use interface in Visual Studio Code . With this tool, you can visualize all your DDEV projects from the sidebar, making it easy to customize each project. Additionally, you can control your project from the sidebar or using the command menu, allowing you to easily switch PHP and NodeJS versions used in your project, as well as manage DDEV services, add or remove services, and quickly access SSH terminals for your running projects. With additional features such as one-click project creation, database snapshot management, configuration file editing, and XDebug enabling/disabling, among others, the extension provides a comprehensive solution for your DDEV development needs. It also offers configuration options that can be found in Visual Studio Code settings and is under constant development, ensuring new features and continuous improvements for an even more efficient development experience.   Drupal 8 JavaScript Snippets by tsega   Drupal 8 JavaScript Snippets by tsega The extension offers useful code snippets in JavaScript extracted from the general documentation of the JavaScript API for Drupal 8 . These snippets include a jQuery wrapper and Drupal 8 behavior, facilitating JavaScript development within Drupal projects. You can access the snippets through the Visual Studio Code command line or by typing the snippet prefixes directly into the code editor window. The snippets are designed to enhance productivity by providing quick access to commonly used JavaScript patterns in Drupal 8 development. Additionally, they are available only in .js extension files. This extension aims to streamline JavaScript coding in Drupal 8 projects, making it easier for developers to implement common functionalities and behaviors.   Drupal 8 Twig Snippets by tsega   Drupal 8 Twig Snippets by tsega This extension adds useful Twig code snippets that can be used with Drupal 8 . You can access the snippets through the Visual Studio Code command line or by typing the snippet prefixes directly into the code editor window. The snippets are designed to enhance productivity by providing quick access to commonly used Twig functions in Drupal 8 theme development. Additionally, they are available only in .twig extension files. This extension aims to streamline Twig programming in Drupal 8 projects, making it easier for developers to implement common functionalities and logic in templates.   Composer by Ioannis Kappas   Composer by Ioannis Kappas This extension provides an interface for the Composer dependency manager in PHP . It also offers schema validation for composer.json configuration files and provides a variety of Composer -compatible commands, such as dependency installation, package updating, autoloader file creation, and more. Additionally, you can customize the extension's settings to enable or disable specific features and define custom working paths.   phpstan by SanderRonde   phpstan by SanderRonde    (Official Extension) The phpstan extension provides an integrated error provider for PHPStan . It runs automatically on your code and highlights errors as you type, in addition to performing analysis across the project and displaying all errors in the Diagnose tab. It also shows variable values according to PHPStan when hovering over them, if the phpstan.enableLanguageServer setting is enabled. You can configure various options, such as the path to the configuration file, the path to your PHP project's root directory, the path to the PHPStan binary, and more. Additionally, you can adjust memory limit, full project timeout, individual file timeout, and other settings. The extension also allows customization of the display, such as enabling or disabling checking on save, showing a progress bar, and enabling the language server to provide information when hovering over code.   gettext by MrOrz   gettext by MrOrz The extension provides support for language files in PO ( Portable Object ), POT ( Template PO ), and POTX ( Compressed Template PO ) formats. It adds syntax highlighting to these files, making them easier to read and edit. Additionally, it displays useful information in the status bar, such as the total number of texts, untranslated texts, and fuzzy texts using the msgfmt --statistics command. It also includes useful keyboard shortcuts for navigating messages, such as moving focus to the next untranslated or fuzzy message, and to the previous one. This extension is useful for developers working with gettext language files ( .po ) and need an integrated tool to assist in editing and managing these files.   gettext-duplicate-error by ovcharik   gettext-duplicate-error by ovcharik This extension highlights duplicate message definitions in .po files of gettext . This is useful for identifying and correcting errors in translation files, as having duplicate messages in a .po file can be problematic. The extension provides a helpful tool for ensuring consistency and accuracy in gettext language files ( .po ).   PHP Debug by Xdebug   PHP Debug by Xdebug    (Official Extension) This extension provides support for debugging PHP code with Xdebug . This makes it easier to detect and correct errors in PHP code by allowing you to set breakpoints, inspect variables, trace program flow, and more. The extension acts as a debugging adapter between Visual Studio Code and Xdebug , which is a PHP extension that needs to be installed on your server. The extension supports a variety of debugging features, such as breakpoints, code stepping, stack tracing, scoped variables, user-defined constants, debug console, watchers, CLI execution, and more. It also offers support for remote debugging on remote hosts and DBGp proxy for multi-user environments. In summary, this extension makes debugging PHP code in Visual Studio Code easier and more efficient by providing powerful tools and features for detecting and fixing issues in your PHP code.   phpfmt - PHP formatter by kokororin   phpfmt - PHP formatter by kokororin The extension integrates phpfmt into the development environment, allowing formatting of PHP code according to standards like PSR1 , PSR2 , and WP , with options to customize indentation, automatically detect type and size of it, and execute PHP . With features like auto-formatting on save, specific rule configuration, and a list of available transformations, it offers a convenient way to maintain consistent and readable coding style in your projects.   PHP DocBlocker by Neil Brayfield   PHP DocBlocker by Neil Brayfield The PHP DocBlocker extension provides a simple and dependency-free way to generate documentation blocks in PHP . It allows auto-completion of documentation blocks when typing /** above a class, function, or class property, as well as insertion of tags like @param , @return , and @throws . Additionally, it can automatically infer parameter and return types from function signatures. The extension also offers configuration options to customize documentation block templates and adjust space between description and tags, among other aspects. With support for different documentation tags and the ability to configure documentation templates according to your needs, this extension simplifies the task of generating consistent and readable documentation in your PHP projects.   php cs fixer by junstyle   php cs fixer by junstyle This extension provides a tool for formatting PHP code and improving its readability. It allows automatically fixing the format of a PHP file using the php-cs-fixer: fix this file command from the command palette or the keyboard shortcut alt + shift + f . It also offers the option to format whole documents or specific selections from the right-click context menu. The extension can be configured according to your preferences, such as the php-cs-fixer executable, formatting rules to apply, and automatic activation on saving the file. Additionally, it provides the ability to automatically install php-cs-fixer or use an existing .phar file. This extension simplifies the formatting process and enhances the consistency of PHP code in your projects.   PHP Namespace Resolver by Mehedi Hassan   PHP Namespace Resolver by Mehedi Hassan The PHP Namespace Resolver extension makes it easy to import and expand namespaces in PHP code. You can import specific classes or all at once, expand imported classes, sort imports by line length or alphabetically, and highlight classes that are not imported or not used. You can also automatically generate the namespace for a file. The extension offers a range of commands that you can search for in the command palette, and you can customize default settings according to your needs, such as excluding global patterns when searching for files, displaying messages in the status bar instead of in a popup window, and automatically sorting imports on saving the file. Additionally, you can assign custom key combinations to quickly access extension commands.     In summary, these extensions not only make my work easier and more efficient in Drupal or PHP projects but also demonstrate the power and versatility of Visual Studio Code as a development platform and code editor. /es/articulos/extensiones-de-visual-studio-code-para-desarrollo-php-y-drupal /en/articles/visual-studio-code-extensions-php-and-drupal-development

full: Prism as a REST API testing server NodeJS API REST Publicado 15/04/2024 Lectura de 5 minutos Galaxy Sphere - Craiyon Galaxy Sphere - Craiyon Craiyon Prism simplifies REST API development by providing a realistic and controlled testing environment, without relying on external servers. An essential tool for REST API developers. Often in the world of development, it becomes a race between the hare and the tortoise, and spoiler alert: you're not the hare. That's the case with REST API development, where API integrations arrive long before the API itself, and you need to provide a testing environment for that hare who's watching you while overtaking you and sends you an email every week asking for a solution. This is where Prism comes into play ( Prisma for friends who don't want to pronounce it with a clenched jaw), an invaluable tool to simplify and streamline the REST API development process. Prism is a REST API simulation server (Among its features) that allows you to define custom endpoints, simulate responses, and set up test scenarios for your applications using the YML interface of OpenAPI . With Prism , development teams can create a realistic and controlled testing environment without relying on external servers or production environments.   Express REST API. Setting up Prism is simple and fast. Once installed, you can easily define endpoints, specify response formats, and simulate different API states such as successful responses, errors, or wait times. Prism offers an intuitive interface that efficiently manages "fake" APIs or test APIs. With Prism, it's possible to define complex test scenarios, simulate dynamic data, and validate application behavior in different situations.   Installation like any other Node.js package. To start using Prism , you first need to install it in your development environment (Obviously). You can install Prism globally using NPM (Node Package Manager) with the following command: npm install -g @stoplight/prism-cli Alternatively, you can omit the -g parameter if you don't want Node packages to proliferate on your machine like rodents. If you need more installation options, you can check Prism's documentation .   Definitions. Once Prism is installed, you can configure it to simulate your REST API. Suppose you have an API with a /users endpoint that returns a list of users in JSON format, the following example YAML configuration file shows how to set up the simulation of this endpoint: openapi: 3.0.0 info: title: Example REST API version: 1.0.0 paths: /users: get: summary: Gets the list of users responses: '200': description: Successful response content: application/json: schema: type: array items: type: object properties: id: type: integer username: type: string email: type: string You can configure this file manually if you feel comfortable with the OpenAPI configuration interface or with any API design tool, such as SwaggerHub , for example.   Start your engines. To run Prism and simulate your REST API, you can do it with the following command (Remember to adjust openapi.yml to the path of the above configuration file): prism mock openapi.yml This will start the test server at the URL http://localhost:4010 , although it accepts the following combinable parameters (The most useful ones): -h: Modifies the IP address to the provided one. For example: prism mock -h 0.0.0.0 openapi.yml -p: Modifies the network port to the provided one. For example: prism mock -p 9999 openapi.yml --dynamic: Generates dynamic responses that match the provided schema. For example: prism mock --dynamic openapi.yml Once the server is started, you can make requests to the service from your machine to the local IP (Or to the IP of the remote machine if installed on a remote server): curl http://localhost:4010/users Prism accepts configurations for GET , POST , PUT , PATCH , and DELETE methods. Conclusion. Prism is an indispensable tool for any development team working with REST APIs. By simplifying the development and testing process, it enables teams to create high-quality applications more quickly and efficiently. With its features and ease of use, Prism has become the perfect companion for any developer looking to improve their API development workflow (Or if you simply don't want to fall behind like the tortoise).   If you need more information about the package, you can check Prism's documentation . /es/articulos/prism-como-servidor-api-rest-de-pruebas /en/articles/prism-rest-api-testing-server

It combines ease of use and technical flexibility, catering to various user needs. FortiClient Download and run. The easiest way to access the Fortinet VPN is to download the FortiClient executable and install it from its official page . Install FortiClient - Step 1 Install FortiClient - Step 1 Initial installation step Install FortiClient - Step 2 Install FortiClient - Step 2 Final installation step This is probably the method recommended by your company's IT department if you are downloading it for work, as it is universal and works on Windows , MacOS , iOS , Linux , and Android at the time of publishing this article. Configuring FortiClient and connecting to the VPN is as simple as following the steps in the graphical interface: Configure FortiClient - Step 1 Configure FortiClient - Step 1 1. First, you need to “ Configure VPN ” Configure FortiClient - Step 2 Configure FortiClient - Step 2 2. Next, you need to enter the VPN name (any name you want), description (any description you want), VPN IP address and port if available, and Fortinet username, although there may be an option to save the password, and click “ Save ” Configure FortiClient - Step 3 Configure FortiClient - Step 3 3. Once the VPN connection is saved, you can access it by checking your Fortinet username and password and clicking the “ Connect ” button Configure FortiClient - Step 4 Configure FortiClient - Step 4 4. To disconnect the VPN, you can use the “ Disconnect ” button While there are many advantages to installing and using the Fortinet FortiClient on Linux , there are also some disadvantages, which are outlined below: Advantages: ➡ Quick and convenient installation. ➡ Cross-platform, with each system having its corresponding installation method. ➡ Easy to configure and use thanks to the graphical interface. Disadvantages: ➡ Depending on your Linux system configuration, you will likely need to enter your Fortinet password each time you want to start the connection. ➡ Neglects the native VPN configuration of Linux and leaves an icon in the system tray (fortitray). ➡ Automation is difficult to configure.   Linux Console What would the penguin's operating system be without its console? The most “Linux” way to access the Fortinet VPN is through the system console, but it requires following a few steps. First, you need to install the Fortinet package, as it likely isn’t installed by default, so execute the following commands in the console: sudo apt update sudo apt install network-manager-fortisslvpn-gnome Next, to connect, you need to provide a security certificate hash. The easiest way to obtain it is by inducing an error with the connection command. To do this, run the following command, replacing IP_ADDRESS , NETWORK_PORT , YOUR_USERNAME , and YOUR_PASSWORD with your Fortinet account values: sudo openfortivpn IP_ADDRESS:NETWORK_PORT --username=YOUR_USERNAME --password=YOUR_PASSWORD This should generate an error in the console output due to the absence of a trusted certificate. Look for a line similar to: ERROR:      --trusted-cert 0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz Each Linux machine has its own trusted certificate hash. To connect, simply repeat the previous command and add the trusted certificate parameter obtained from the error: sudo openfortivpn IP_ADDRESS:NETWORK_PORT --username=YOUR_USERNAME --password=YOUR_PASSWORD --trusted-cert 0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz   While there are many advantages to installing and using the Fortinet VPN via the Linux console, there are also some disadvantages, which are outlined below: Advantages: ➡ Quick installation via console. ➡ Connection can be automated. ➡ Does not require the system's graphical interface. (Advantage and disadvantage) Disadvantages: ➡ Requires using the Linux console. ➡ Complex to use. ➡ Does not require the system's graphical interface. (Advantage and disadvantage)   Linux Network Connections Like any other network connection. Adding the Fortinet VPN to the list of Linux networks is probably the most convenient way to connect, as it is added as a VPN to your WiFi networks, and connecting is as simple as accessing a WiFi network. The graphical layout and texts of the configurations vary depending on the Linux distribution. For this guide, I will use Kubuntu 22.04 LTS . First, install the Fortinet package, as it is likely not installed by default. Execute the following commands in the console: sudo apt update sudo apt install network-manager-fortisslvpn-gnome Next, to configure the VPN connection, you need to provide a security certificate hash. The easiest way to obtain it is by inducing an error with the connection command. To do this, run the following command, replacing IP_ADDRESS , NETWORK_PORT , YOUR_USERNAME , and YOUR_PASSWORD with your Fortinet account values: sudo openfortivpn IP_ADDRESS:NETWORK_PORT --username=YOUR_USERNAME --password=YOUR_PASSWORD This should generate an error in the console output due to the absence of a trusted certificate. Look for a line similar to: ERROR:      --trusted-cert 0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz Copy the trusted certificate hash obtained from the error, as it will be needed later. Now, you need to create the VPN connection. You can access the network connection settings from system settings or by right-clicking on the WiFi icon in the taskbar. Once in the settings, look for the “ + ” button or “ Add new connection ” and a window with multiple connection options will open. Under the “ VPN Connections ” group or section, select a connection called “ Fortinet SSLVPN (fortisslvpn) ” and click “ Create ”. This will open the VPN network configuration window. For the connection name, you can choose any value you prefer; this will later appear in the network connections along with the VPN connection type icon. The gateway should be the VPN IP address, and if you have a port, it should be included after the IP address separated by “:”, resulting in “ IP_ADDRESS:NETWORK_PORT ”. The username and password should be the values of your Fortinet account. Depending on the Linux distribution, there will be sections, tabs, or buttons that open windows. After configuring “ Advanced ”, include the hash you copied from the console error in the trusted certificate field. After configuring “ IPv4 ” > “ Routes ”, you should check the “ Use only for resources on this connection ” option to prevent it from affecting your other network connections. After saving the VPN connection configuration, it should appear alongside the WiFi networks in its own section in settings, or with all connections if you click the network icon in the taskbar. To connect, simply click the “ Connect ” button. While there are many advantages to installing and using the Fortinet VPN through Linux networks, there are also some disadvantages, which are outlined below: Advantages: ➡ Once installed, its use is very straightforward. ➡ Does not require open windows during connection. ➡ The interface integrates with the Linux distribution. Disadvantages: ➡ Requires using the Linux console. ➡ Complex to configure and varies depending on the Linux distribution. ➡ Automation is difficult to configure.     Conclusion. Fortinet offers various options for configuring and using its VPN on multiple platforms. Its installation is straightforward and quick, especially through the official FortiClient client, and is notable for its ease of use thanks to an intuitive graphical interface. However, Linux users have additional alternatives, such as using the console and integrating with the system’s network connections, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. Overall, it is a versatile tool that adapts to different user needs and preferences, with configuration methods that balance ease of use and technical flexibility.   /es/articulos/configurar-vpn-de-fortinet-en-linux /en/articles/configure-fortinet-vpn-linux

I will show you how to install and use it efficiently in your projects. SASS ( Syntactically Awesome Style Sheets ) or Super CSS for friends ( SIUUUUUUUSS in Portuguese), allows for automatic compilation of component-based styles for web theme creation. This system is quite useful for unifying the CSS file of a web page to reduce file transfer and improve performance (One step closer to getting a 100/100 score from Google Lighthouse ).   Quick, easy, and for the whole family. The first thing to do is to install Node , the main executor of SASS . It's best to follow the steps on the official Node page for the environment you need: https://nodejs.org/en/download/package-manager . Now that Node is working correctly on your machine (or should be), it's time to install SASS . You can install it globally on the whole machine (recommended for testing) as recommended in the official SASS documentation : npm install -g sass Or you can install SASS in the project where you will use the package from the root folder of the package (don't forget to run the Node project initiation command npm init first): npm install sass   Execution time is shorter than expected. Compiling the file is quite simple; the sass command accepts various parameters, but the most useful ones (probably) are the input path SCSS , the output path CSS , the style parameter for compiling expanded or compressed styles ( expanded (default) or compressed ), and the watch parameter to automatically compile whenever it detects a saved change in the SCSS files. An example of how the command looks with these parameters applied is: npx sass --watch --style=compressed path/to/file.scss:path/to/file.css In this example, SASS is instructed to compile the main SCSS file in a compressed format (the one that usually contains all the dependencies) and to compile the compressed result into the CSS file at the specified path. If you need more configurations, here is the output of sass --help : Compile Sass to CSS. Only valid with --watch. --[no-]stop-on-error Don't compile more files once an error is encountered. -i, --interactive Run an interactive SassScript shell. -c, --[no-]color Whether to use terminal colors for messages. --[no-]unicode Whether to use Unicode characters for messages. --[no-]trace Print full Dart stack traces for exceptions. -h, --help Print this usage information. --version Print the version of Dart Sass.   In a real example, let's consider the following unoptimized CSS file without SASS : body { font: Helvetica, sans-serif; color: #333; } This file takes up 54 bytes , and if more styles with the same color or font need to be added, a copy of the same style would be required, which is cumbersome for the developer. Now, I convert this CSS file to SCSS : $font-stack: Helvetica, sans-serif; $primary-color: #333; body { font: $font-stack; color: $primary-color; } And upon compiling it with compression, this is the result: body{font:Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#333} It takes up 43 bytes , and the developer does not need to bother decompressing it to edit it, as the styles are configured from the SCSS file.   In the previous examples, the size difference may not seem significant, but when scaled to larger projects, the difference becomes considerable, and the convenience of using variables becomes more necessary. Another example of the advantages of SASS is element nesting. Multiple child elements can be nested under the same parent umbrella. The following CSS file has many nestings that, during development, can be confusing and lead to errors, causing styles to not function correctly because the element to be selected is not properly recognized: body element.class__one#id-element .class__one__two { font: $font-stack; color: $primary-color; } When converted to SASS , it is evident that the nestings improve the readability of the styles: $font-stack: Helvetica, sans-serif; $primary-color: #333; body { element { &.class { &__one { &#id-element { .class { &__two { font: $font-stack; color: $primary-color; } } } } } } }     Conclusion. These examples are just the tip of the iceberg that makes SASS improve style development. It is best to read the official SASS documentation to see all the tool's possibilities. They also have an online compiler so you can test the CSS code before migrating your project.   /es/articulos/optimizacion-y-compilacion-automatica-de-estilos-web-con-sass /en/articles/optimization-and-automatic-compilation-web-styles-sass

full: Migrate Content Paragraphs with Migrate Drupal Migrate Publicado 18/03/2024 Actualizado 29/05/2024 Lectura de 20 minutos How do birds know how to migrate? - The Daily Illini How do birds know how to migrate? - The Daily Illini How do birds know how to migrate? - The Daily Illini Content migration between different versions of Drupal can be a challenging task, especially when facing changes in data structure such as the introduction of Paragraphs. This process requires a meticulous approach and deep understanding of entity relationships. With a solid understanding and the right tools, successful migrations are achievable. The other day I was proposed to migrate content from a website on Drupal 7 to another on Drupal 10 simply because it was easier to renovate it than to update it. And I, being an expert in saying yes without knowing the swamp I was getting into, started analyzing how I could do it. In search of enlightenment. In the meantime, the idea arose to build a view in Drupal 7 that provides absolutely all the fields of a content type in JSON format. So far, so simple, right? You configure a YML file for migration with the appropriate plugins, and there you go, the entities were copied from one system to another. It turns out that the data structure has changed in the last 10 years (What a surprise), and now certain content blocks that used to be stored in the entity itself are stored as Paragraph type entities. I thought, okay, I'll migrate the Paragraph entities, add the migration as a dependency of the main entity, and add the migration plugin, and nothing happened here. Then I encountered a wonderful bidirectionality here: The parent entity needed to have the Paragraph referenced, and the Paragraph needed to have the parent entity referenced (along with other parent data). The problem was that I couldn't migrate it like this with the default migrate plugin because it only added the reference in one of the entities: If I added the Paragraph as a dependency of the entity, this did not have a reference to the parent, and vice versa. This battle lasted three long days until I came up with a solution worthy of Miguel Ángel (For sculpting and all that): Chisel the database when migrating Paragraphs so that both entities matched. NOTE : The process of migrating entities with the inclusion of paragraphs is a complex task that requires a meticulous approach and a deep understanding of data structure and entity relationships. In this extension, we will delve into the different aspects involved in this process, from identifying associated paragraphs to updating the database and verifying the integrity of the migrated data.   Getting hands dirty. In order to have all the data post migration, it was best to create an Event Subscriber, starting with the basic configuration in the module.services.yml file: services: module.migration_finished_subscriber: class: Drupal\module\EventSubscriber\MigrateParagraphsEventSubscriber tags: - { name: event_subscriber } And its corresponding class in the src/EventSubscriber/MigrateParagraphsEventSubscriber.php file: class MigrateParagraphsEventSubscriber implements EventSubscriberInterface { public static function getSubscribedEvents() { $events[MigrateEvents::POST_IMPORT][] = ['postImport']; return $events; } public function postImport(MigrateImportEvent $event) { } } With this configuration and a cache flush, after running any migration, the code of the postImport method will be executed.   Leaving breadcrumbs. Now, we need to identify the migration processes of Paragraphs in the parent entity, in order to have both entities consolidated in the database: The parent entity, and the Paragraph. For this, the simplest thing is to add an identifying property to the process: field_paragraphs/target_id: plugin: migration_lookup migration: module_migrate_paragraphs migrate_paragraphs: true source: id From this configuration, the ID of the entities migrated in the first migration (the Paragraphs) would be obtained based on a common ID from the data source, with the added property migrate_paragraphs: true to identify in the process that this process requires matching the Paragraph entities from the previous migration with those migrated in the current configuration. Getting hands dirty. Now we need to identify the fields that require a Paragraph migration. To do this, we need to obtain the migration object from the event, and its process in array format: $migration = $event->getMigration(); $migration_process = $migration->getProcess(); Now comes the fun part, "processing the process": protected function searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray(array $values, string|int $key = 0, string $value = ''): mixed { foreach ($values as $vkey => $vvalue) { if ($vkey === $key && $vvalue == $value) { return $vkey;  }  else {  if (is_array($vvalue)) {  $found = $this->searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray($vvalue, $key, $value);  if ($this->paragraph_path_found === TRUE) {  $this->paragraph_fields[$vkey] = [  'field' => $vkey,  'migration' => $found,  ];  $this->paragraph_path_found = FALSE;  }  if ($found === $key) {  $this->paragraph_path_found = TRUE;  return (!empty($vvalue['migration'])) ? $vvalue['migration'] : $values;  }  }  }  }  return ''; } This wonderful method iterates recursively over all processes in an array, and saves the field name of those containing the property migrate_paragraphs: true in the list $this->paragraph_fields .   Now is when the real marriage between the parent entity and the child paragraphs begins, after iterating and filtering the obtained fields: foreach ($this->paragraph_fields as $paragraph_field) { if (empty($paragraph_field['field']) || empty($paragraph_field['migration'])) { continue; } if (preg_match($this->match_field_name_regex, $paragraph_field['field'], $matches)) { foreach ($matches as $field_name) { if (!preg_match($this->match_field_name_regex, $field_name)) { Subsequently, the ID of the parent entity is obtained from the referenced table of migrated entities (This must be iterated for security despite assuming that it is a 1:1 relationship in most contexts, it would be an error of abstract definition not to do so): $source = $this->database->select('migrate_map_' . $migration->id(), 'mm') ->fields('mm', [$this->migrate_db_target_id_column, $this->migrate_db_source_id_column]) ->execute() ->fetchAllAssoc($this->migrate_db_target_id_column); foreach ($source as $source_data) { if (!empty($source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}) && !empty($source_data->{$this->migrate_db_source_id_column})) { $entity = NULL;   Red pill, blue pill. It is important to note that this process only provided us with the ID of the entity, which can be of any type, so it must be parsed from the configuration of the destination plugin or Destination Plug-in the ID of the entity type on which we must load the ID we obtained. For this, there are two methods, one more reliable than the other, although for this example I have included both to ensure their obtainment. The first method consists of obtaining through regular expression the value of the ID of the Destination Plug-in the rightmost value, coinciding in 99.99% of cases (Source: Times New Roman) with the entity type, of course, in most cases coinciding with the value " node ". To see it better, the regular expression obtains the highlighted value of "entity: node ", making it possible through Entity Type Manager to obtain the node by its ID. If this process is not possible, the Entity Type Manager would throw an exception in which we will process the second less reliable method: Obtaining the provider of the definition of the Destination Plug-in, this method can fail in the case of sub entities like Paragraphs , so it is best to start with the first method. The try-catch defined in the following block explains how to implement both methods and resort to the second in case of failure of the first: $migration_destination_plugin = $migration->getDestinationPlugin(); $migration_destination_plugin_definition = $migration_destination_plugin->getPluginDefinition(); try { preg_match($this->match_entity_regex, $migration_destination_plugin_definition['id'], $entity_type); $entity_type = $entity_type[1]; $entity = \Drupal::entityTypeManager()->getStorage($entity_type)->load($source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}); } catch (InvalidPluginDefinitionException|PluginNotFoundException|\Exception $e) { if (!empty($migration_destination_plugin_definition['provider'])) { $entity = \Drupal::entityTypeManager()->getStorage($entity_type)->load($source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}); } } if ($entity instanceof FieldableEntityInterface) {   The icing on the cake. Finally, the ID of the Paragraphs that must be matched with the parent entity is obtained from the referenced table of migrated entities. The language to associate the Paragraph is loaded, by default it can be associated with the main language of the site, and the corresponding value of the base data table of Paragraphs is updated to establish the parent entity, the language of the Paragraph, and some more data. $paragraphs = $this->database->select('migrate_map_' . $paragraph_field['migration'], 'mm') ->condition('mm.'. $this->migrate_db_source_id_column, $source_data->{$this->migrate_db_source_id_column}) ->fields('mm', [$this->migrate_db_target_id_column, $this->migrate_db_source_id_column]) ->execute() ->fetchAllAssoc($this->migrate_db_target_id_column); foreach ($paragraphs as $paragraphs_source_data) { if (!empty($paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column})) { $default_language = $this->language_manager->getDefaultLanguage(); $default_language_id = $default_language->getId(); $entity_langcode = ($entity->hasField('langcode') && $entity->langcode->value) ? $entity->langcode->value : 'und'; $this->database->update('paragraphs_item_field_data') ->fields([ 'langcode' => $entity_langcode, 'parent_id' => $source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}, 'parent_type' => $entity_type, 'default_langcode' => ($default_language_id == $entity_langcode) ? 1 : 0, 'parent_field_name' => $field_name, 'content_translation_source' => $default_language_id, ]) ->condition('id', $paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}) ->execute(); And, although this task has been theoretically performed by Migrate, to put the icing on the cake, we load the paragraph and associate it with the field of the parent entity if it is not already. $paragraph = Paragraph::load($paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}); if ($paragraph instanceof ParagraphInterface && $entity->hasField($field_name) && !$this->isParagrahDuplicated($entity, $paragraph, $field_name)) { $entity->{$field_name}->appendItem($paragraph); $entity->save(); Conclusion. Content migration, especially when it involves complex entities like Paragraphs in Drupal, can be a challenging process. However, with a solid understanding of the processes involved and the available tools, successful migrations are possible.   Code. If you need it, you can view the complete code analyzed in this article on this GitHub Gist .     May 9, 2024 Update Since I published this article (and previously completed this development), I've had a nagging feeling of code improvement. That's why we have decided to do tests by rewriting the searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray() method from scratch. The simplest is the most efficient. Really, the best way to avoid the use of class attributes is by using the extreme simplification of the method's own recursion so that the recursion itself does not delay the process: protected function searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray(array $values, string $value, string $field = '', string $key = 'migrate_paragraphs'): array { $paragraphs_found_list = []; foreach ($values as $vkey => $vvalue) { if (is_array($vvalue)) { if (is_string($vkey) && strlen($vkey) > 0) { $field = $vkey; } $paragraphs_found_list = array_merge($paragraphs_found_list, $this->searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray($vvalue, $value, $field, $key)); } elseif ($vkey === $key && (string) $vvalue === $value && isset($values['migration']) && is_string($values['migration'])) { $paragraphs_found_list[$field] = [ 'migration' => $values['migration'], ]; continue; } } return $paragraphs_found_list; } This allows eliminating the attributes related to the $this->identifier , $this->paragraph_fields , and $this->paragraph_path_found method. You also need to update the initial method call to adapt it to the results and the return variable, which will now always be of type array , replacing $this->searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray($migration_process, $this->identifier, TRUE); if (!empty($this->paragraph_fields)) { foreach ($this->paragraph_fields as $paragraph_field) { if (empty($paragraph_field['field']) || empty($paragraph_field['migration'])) { continue; } if (preg_match($this->match_field_name_regex, $paragraph_field['field'], $matches)) { with $paragraph_fields = $this->searchMigrationParagraphKeyValueInProcessArray($migration_process, (string) TRUE); if (!empty($paragraph_fields)) { foreach ($paragraph_fields as $paragraph_field_name => $paragraph_field) { if (!is_string($paragraph_field_name) || !is_string($paragraph_field['migration'])) { continue; } if (preg_match($this->match_field_name_regex, $paragraph_field_name, $matches)) {   Additionally, as an improvement, you can apply the $this->migrate_db_prefix attribute (which was not being applied with the value "migrate_map_" ); and as a bug fix, you can remove the $this->match_entity_regex attribute since it was only used once (It's best to apply the regular expression or RegEx directly as a string within the PHP preg_match function).   Code. If you need it, the complete code analyzed in this article update can be seen on this GitHub Gist .     Update from May 29, 2024 After conducting multiple migration tests for different types of entities, there were cases where an error occurred in the row because the entity was skipped in different scenarios (entity translation, nested paragraphs, etc.), something I have corrected. It's better to let go than to hold on to the fatal error. In reality, debugging code is very healthy and saves a lot of time (even if it is not always pleasant). This led me to the last block of code, where the database is chiseled so that the paragraph does not become orphaned, and the parent entity is updated so that it does not remain childless. In specific cases where it cannot find the child's ID, it tries to update both and then ends the process, losing the entity and risking the continuity of the migration. if (!empty($paragraphs)) { foreach ($paragraphs as $paragraphs_source_data) { if (!empty($paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column})) { // It is assumed that the website's default language is the same as the entity's default language. // This is used only to define if the Paragraph translation is the default translation. /** @var \Drupal\Core\Language\LanguageInterface $default_language */ $default_language = $this->language_manager->getDefaultLanguage(); $default_language_id = $default_language->getId(); $entity_langcode = ($entity->hasField('langcode') && $entity->langcode->value) ? $entity->langcode->value : 'und'; // Update the Paragraph values to have the entity field as parent. $this->database->update('paragraphs_item_field_data') ->fields([ 'langcode' => $entity_langcode, 'parent_id' => $source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}, 'parent_type' => $entity_type, 'default_langcode' => ($default_language_id == $entity_langcode) ? 1 : 0, 'parent_field_name' => $field_name, 'content_translation_source' => $default_language_id, ]) ->condition('id', $paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}) ->execute(); /** @var \Drupal\paragraphs\ParagraphInterface|null $paragraph */ $paragraph = Paragraph::load($paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}); // For security reasons, check that the reference to the Paragraph // in the entity field is not duplicated and consolidate its reference. if ($paragraph instanceof ParagraphInterface && $entity->hasField($field_name) && !$this->isParagrahDuplicated($entity, $paragraph, $field_name)) { $entity->{$field_name}->appendItem($paragraph); $entity->save(); } } } }   The best solution has been implemented for a long time. The best way to detect errors and continue the migration without major incidents is to implement in this case a try-catch both in chiseling the database and updating the parent entity. But going a step further and improving the system to perform fewer database updates, chiseling can be included after validating the existence of the paragraph, thus avoiding repetitions and unnecessary updates, replacing the previous block with: if (!empty($paragraphs)) { foreach ($paragraphs as $paragraphs_source_data) { if (!empty($paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column})) { /** @var \Drupal\paragraphs\ParagraphInterface|null $paragraph */ $paragraph = Paragraph::load($paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}); // For security reasons, check that the reference to the Paragraph // in the entity field is not duplicated and consolidate its reference. if ($paragraph instanceof ParagraphInterface && $entity->hasField($field_name) && !$this->isParagrahDuplicated($entity, $paragraph, $field_name)) { try { // It is assumed that the website's default language is the same as the entity's default language. // This is used only to define if the Paragraph translation is the default translation. /** @var \Drupal\Core\Language\LanguageInterface $default_language */ $default_language = $this->language_manager->getDefaultLanguage(); $default_language_id = $default_language->getId(); $entity_langcode = ($entity->hasField('langcode') && $entity->langcode->value) ? $entity->langcode->value : 'und'; // Update the Paragraph values to have the entity field as parent. $this->database->update('paragraphs_item_field_data') ->fields([ 'langcode' => $entity_langcode, 'parent_id' => $source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}, 'parent_type' => $entity_type, 'default_langcode' => ($default_language_id == $entity_langcode) ? 1 : 0, 'parent_field_name' => $field_name, 'content_translation_source' => $default_language_id, ]) ->condition('id', $paragraphs_source_data->{$this->migrate_db_target_id_column}) ->execute(); } catch (\Exception $e) { $this->logger->error($e->getMessage()); } try { $entity->{$field_name}->appendItem($paragraph); $entity->save(); } catch (\Exception $e) { $this->logger->error($e->getMessage()); } } } } } Within the catch, you can see the implementation of Drupal's logger system. To add it, it is as simple as adding the service @logger.factory to the event subscriber in the services.yml file, adding the dependency Drupal\Core\Logger\LoggerChannelFactory to the event subscriber , including within this the object to log errors /** * The logger channel. * * @var \Drupal\Core\Logger\LoggerChannelInterface */ protected $logger; and updating the class constructor to associate the service with the object: /** * Constructor. * * @param \Drupal\Core\Database\Connection $database * The database connection. * @param \Drupal\Core\Logger\LoggerChannelFactory $logger * The logger channel. * @param \Drupal\Core\Language\LanguageManagerInterface $language_manager * The language manager. * @param \Drupal\Core\Entity\EntityTypeManagerInterface $entity_type_manager * The entity type manager. */ public function __construct(Connection $database, LoggerChannelFactory $logger, LanguageManagerInterface $language_manager, EntityTypeManagerInterface $entity_type_manager) { $this->database = $database; $this->language_manager = $language_manager; $this->logger = $logger->get('module'); $this->entity_type_manager = $entity_type_manager; } This last step is optional. If you do not want to log errors during the migration, you can simply leave the catch empty.   Code. full: Error 500 on the entity fields management page in Drupal Drupal Error Publicado 08/09/2024 Lectura de 5 minutos A close-up of a street sign surrounded by leaves - Photo by Justin Little on Unsplash A close-up of a street sign surrounded by leaves - Photo by Justin Little on Unsplash A close-up of a street sign surrounded by leaves - Photo by Justin Little on Unsplash Sometimes, a small line of code can trigger major issues. In the past week, an unexpected 500 error in a local environment with Drupal 10 led to a lengthy search for solutions. Last week I wrote a single line of code. It doesn't seem like much—some say the best programmers write the least—but the downside is that it was a line of code in a YML file. This story is worthy of Dj Marmota with the lamp and the store clerk (But less aggressive): Dj Marmota - Ignacio Francolino - YouTube thumbnail Dj Marmota - Ignacio Francolino - YouTube thumbnail - I turn on the lamp, boom! Short circuit! I grab the bike, easy, boom! boom! boom! boom! I head to the hardware store, and I say: - Give me one of those things that goes ticky-ticky for the lamp, pi, the guy gives it to me. - How do I replace it? I ask. + It’s easy, he says, take off the knob, click, put in the replacement, pi. - Do you take cards? + No!, click-click! - I give him forty, the guy, ping!, gives me 20. - You owe me $30, I say, and the guy starts with the taxes, blah blah, I’ll give you 20. - $20, pssh! From where? + Well, if you don’t like it, get lost! - Oh yeah? Right then I go smack!, the guy, boom!, and we start, smack smack! I hit him on the nose, grab him by the neck, start boom! boom! boom! boom! boom! against the counter, grab the change, and I'm out!       A hidden 500 error. My story begins when, in the local environment of a project using DDEV and Drupal 10 , I started creating a content type and adding fields to it. After adding ten or fifteen fields, a mix of reused and new ones, I created two specific fields ( Text (long with format) and Entity Reference: Paragraph ), and as they say in the video above: " Boom! Short circuit! "—the screen showed a 500 error on all field management pages of the node entity type /admin/structure/types/manage/*/fields : Error 500 in Google Chrome browser Error 500 in Google Chrome browser   This error only happens on the field management pages of the node entity type, and only when adding those two specific fields, which led me to suspect it was a local issue. Although I was hesitant to push the configuration to other environments, this type of error often stems from communication or processing issues between different web technologies. So, I made a quick Google search, which yielded no helpful results. After about twenty thousand attempts with different fields (changing the machine name, label, format, or reference, disabling translations in the case of the text), and being able to add other types of fields, it seemed like the battle was lost.     Google search uncovered great things. Indeed, the initial search for this problem should have led me to a quick solution on drupal.org or StackOverflow . Instead, I ignored the most text-heavy result, only to later give it another chance out of desperation to fix this 500 error. And I ended up at 500 Internal Server Error , specifically the glorious comment I was looking for: #12 , which indicates that in the site's .services.yml files, you need to set the parameter http.response.debug_cacheability_headers to FALSE or remove the line altogether.   To the point. Searching through the project's code, I found the file sites/development.services.yml with the following content: # Local development services. # # To activate this feature, follow the instructions at the top of the # 'example.settings.local.php' file, which sits next to this file. parameters: http.response.debug_cacheability_headers: true services: cache.backend.null: class: Drupal\Core\Cache\NullBackendFactory I had a poker face but was also relieved when I saw the parameter mentioned in the comment with the opposite value to what was recommended to fix this bug. So, I replaced the parameter value with FALSE , leaving the file content as follows: # Local development services. # # To activate this feature, follow the instructions at the top of the # 'example.settings.local.php' file, which sits next to this file. parameters: http.response.debug_cacheability_headers: false services: cache.backend.null: class: Drupal\Core\Cache\NullBackendFactory And… drum roll… it works! Thus ending a week of stress and anxiety with this problem on a local branch. Indeed, this issue only affects the local environment because in all other remote environments, this parameter was correctly configured. However, the problem was still significant since fields are usually created locally. In any case, all's well that ends well.     What is the parameter for? The http.response.debug_cacheability_headers parameter in Drupal enables the inclusion of additional headers in HTTP responses to display information about how page cacheability is managed. When enabled, Drupal adds headers such as X-Drupal-Cache-Tags , X-Drupal-Cache-Contexts , and X-Drupal-Cache-Max-Age , which indicate what elements affect the cache, under what contexts it varies (e.g., language or user), and how long a response can be cached. This feature is useful in development or debugging environments to optimize cache usage, as it allows developers to visualize how contexts, cache tags, and the lifetime of a page are managed, making it easier to identify performance issues or cache invalidation errors. However, it should be disabled in production because it generates additional headers that are unnecessary and may impact performance.     Conclusion. What seemed like a small technical detail triggered a series of unexpected challenges, reflecting how unpredictable web development can be. This experience highlights that sometimes the solution to a complex problem may depend on a single line of code, in this case within a YML configuration file—something easily overlooked. Situations like these remind us of the importance of patience in solving errors without tossing the computer out the window. Although the experience can be frustrating, in the end, solving these issues is what makes programming so rewarding.   /es/articulos/error-500-en-la-pagina-de-gestion-de-campos-de-entidad-de-drupal /en/articles/error-500-entity-fields-management-page-drupal

You might wonder, why choose Drupal for a static site when there are other more specific options available? Well, Drupal is known for its robustness and its ability to effectively handle complex projects. With Tome's help, we can transform a dynamic Drupal website into a static, easily distributable, and quickly loadable version. This is ideal for websites that don't require frequent updates and can benefit from the speed and security of static sites. In the ever-evolving world of web development, creating static sites has become a popular choice due to its performance, security, and ease of implementation. Decoupled Drupal and Tome. Decoupled Drupal is an architecture that separates the presentation layer (front-end) from the logic and data (back-end). This means that Drupal is used only as a content management system and is not directly linked to the user interface. On the other hand, Tome is a tool that allows exporting Drupal websites as static HTML files, making them independent of a back-end server. Setting up a site with Decoupled Drupal. Start by installing Drupal in the traditional way. You can download Drupal files from its official website and follow the installation instructions (Old school, let's go), although you can install it in a way that suits you best. Once Drupal is installed, configure your content and structure as you wish. This may include creating content, configuring content types, and building views.   Implementing Tome. Use Composer to install the Tome library in your Drupal project. This can be done by running the following command in the command line: composer require drupal/tome Once the Tome library is installed and the Drupal module is enabled, you can generate the static files of your Drupal website by running the following command: drush tome:export This command will generate a static version of your Drupal site in a specified folder. Implementation and deployment. Set up a web server to serve the static files generated by Tome. You can use any web server that supports static files, such as Apache , Nginx , or even GitHub Pages . Copy the static files generated by Tome into the root directory of your web server. Once this is done, your decoupled Drupal website will be available at your server's URL. Benefits of a static website with Drupal and Tome. A static website created with Drupal and Tome offers several significant benefits. Firstly, it notably improves the site's performance by loading faster, as it eliminates the need for server-side processing. Additionally, it provides an additional layer of security by reducing potential vulnerability points by removing server logic. Lastly, it simplifies the deployment process by generating static files with Tome, thus eliminating the need to rely on a back-end server. This combination offers a powerful and flexible solution for creating high-performance static websites.     For more information, you can consult the Tome documentation . /es/articulos/montar-y-exportar-un-sitio-web-estatico-con-drupal-desacoplado-y-tome /en/articles/building-and-exporting-static-website-decoupled-drupal-and-tome

In the article Prism As A REST API Testing Server I delve into the installation and basic configuration of Prism , so in this article, I will skip the installation and validation process that Prism uses with OpenAPI definitions.   Using Prism as a REST API proxy has the main advantage of validating requests against the port, but it is also important to note that this functionality redirects all requests to a single REST API port, which can be challenging if you have more than one port in your functionality. This concept is easier to understand with the following diagrams:   Prism As A Validation Proxy API Server - The proxy receives requests to multiple REST API ports and redirects them to a single real port Prism As A Validation Proxy API Server - The proxy receives requests to multiple REST API ports and redirects them to a single real port The proxy receives requests to multiple REST API ports and redirects them to a single real port.   Prism As A Validation Proxy API Server - The proxy receives requests to a single REST API port and redirects them to the real port, facilitating development Prism As A Validation Proxy API Server - The proxy receives requests to a single REST API port and redirects them to the real port, facilitating development The proxy receives requests to a single REST API port and redirects them to the real port, facilitating development.     Intercepting requests with Prism's network. With this clear, setting up the proxy is as simple as running the following command: prism proxy openapi.yaml https://www.example.com/api/v1/port/   Although Prism allows configuring some proxy settings via parameters, below are the most useful ones: --errors: Recommended parameter. The response to the request generates an error if it does not validate with the definitions. For example: prism proxy openapi.yaml https://www.example.com/api/v1/port/ --errors -h: Changes the IP address to the one provided. For example: prism proxy -h 0.0.0.0 openapi.yaml https://www.example.com/api/v1/port/ -p: Changes the network port to the one provided. For example: prism proxy -p 9999 openapi.yaml https://www.example.com/api/v1/port/ -m: Enables multiprocessing. Recommended parameter if the proxy is going to receive many requests. For example: prism proxy -m openapi.yaml https://www.example.com/api/v1/port/   Once the server is started, you can make requests to the service from your machine to the local IP (or to the IP of the remote machine if installed on a remote server): curl http://localhost:4010/users Prism accepts configurations for GET , POST , PUT , PATCH , and DELETE methods.     What happens at the real REST API port? Debugging the request at the real REST API port, you can verify that the proxy has made the request against the port, sending the query parameter “q” with the URL of the port to interact with. For example, if you have a REST API port /users/delete that performs an action with the DELETE method on a user ID in the body {id: 1} , when making the request against the Prism proxy, it validates the request and forwards it to the real REST API port /api/v1/port as /api/v1/port?q=/users/delete with the DELETE method and the request body {id: 1} . The port returns a status code and a message in the body that is transferred to the proxy, and then the proxy returns to the client:   Prism As A Validation Proxy API Server - The proxy returns the requests from the real port, or a validation error according to the OpenAPI definitions. Prism emerges as a valuable tool for validating and redirecting REST API requests, functioning as an effective proxy that ensures requests comply with OpenAPI definitions before being processed by the real REST API port. This not only simplifies the workflow by intercepting and validating requests but also enhances the robustness of applications through strict adherence to the REST API specifications, resulting in a more secure and efficient development process.   If you need more information about the package, you can check Prism's documentation .   /es/articulos/prism-como-servidor-api-proxy-de-validacion /en/articles/prism-validation-proxy-api-server
