full: Compile, compress, and improve the compatibility of JavaScript files with Babel NodeJS JavaScript Babel Publicado 06/07/2024 Lectura de 7 minutos The Tower of Babel represented together with the logos of JavaScript and different browsers The Tower of Babel represented together with the logos of JavaScript and different browsers The automatic compilation, compression, and optimization of JavaScript is an essential practice for improving web page performance. In the article Automatic Web Styles Optimization and Compilation with SASS I talk about CSS file compilation and compression and how reducing file transfer rates impacts web performance. Unlike CSS files, JavaScript files offer more compression possibilities, and their compilation improves compatibility across different browser versions.   Getting Started. The first step is to install Node , the primary executor of Babel . It’s best to follow the steps on the official Node page for your required environment: https://nodejs.org/en/download/package-manager . Now that Node is working correctly on the machine (or should be), it's time to install Babel in the project. In the official documentation , it is recommended to save all packages in the development section with the --save-dev parameter, but I'll leave that decision up to you (don't forget to run the Node project initiation command npm init first): npm install @babel/core npm install @babel/preset-env And if you want to compress JavaScript files, I recommend installing the compression package: npm install babel-preset-minify   Basic Configuration. Babel works with environments called " presets ". You can create your own, but it's more convenient to use a published one . Among the previously installed packages are the basic Babel preset ( @babel/preset-env ) and the compression preset ( babel-preset-minify ). The Babel configuration file should be (or is usually) named babel.config.json , and it should have the following minimum structure: { "targets": "", "presets": [], "plugins": [] } The targets element is a string or an array of strings referring to browser compatibility. Its configuration is as simple as including, for example, "last 3 versions" so that the JavaScript code is compiled with compatibility for the last 3 versions of all browsers (this element is actually requests to the API browserslist-compatible of caveats ). It’s not a mandatory element, but it simplifies your first steps with Babel ; the presets element is an array of strings indicating the presets you will use during the compilation process. With the previously installed ones, the value of this element should be: { "presets": [ "@babel/preset-env", "minify" ], } And finally, the plugins element. This array of strings contains all the community Babel plug-ins or add-ons that will be used during the compilation process. Plug-ins are very useful for extending Babel 's functionality, and this public repository collects many of them. In the end, you should have a babel.config.json file that looks like this: { "targets": "last 3 versions", "presets": [ "@babel/preset-env", "minify" ], "plugins": [] }   Testing the Setup. To run Babel , there are countless parameters you'll find in the documentation, but the most relevant for starting is knowing that by default it requires a path to the JavaScript directory or file, and if you don't want to mess up your wonderful code, I recommend using the --out-dir parameter with an output directory: npx babel path/to/js/directory --out-dir path/to/output/js/directory But it's best to see it with a real example, using the above configuration file and the following JavaScript code: // Function to change the text of an element. function changeText() { document.getElementById("demo-text").innerText = "Text changed!"; } // Function to show an alert. function showAlert() { alert("Hello! This is an alert."); } // Function to add two numbers and print the result in the DOM. function sumNumbers() { let num1 = parseInt(document.getElementById("num1").value); let num2 = parseInt(document.getElementById("num2").value); let sum = num1 + num2; document.getElementById("result").innerText = "The sum is: " + sum; } // Event to change the body background color. function changeBackgroundColor() { document.body.style.backgroundColor = "#f0f0f0"; } // Add events to buttons when the page loads. window.onload = function() { document.getElementById("change-text-btn").addEventListener("click", changeText); document.getElementById("alert-btn").addEventListener("click", showAlert); document.getElementById("sum-btn").addEventListener("click", sumNumbers); document.getElementById("change-bg-btn").addEventListener("click", changeBackgroundColor); } This takes up 1.1 KiB , but after compiling it with Babel , this is the result: "use strict";// Function to change the text of an element. function changeText(){document.getElementById("demo-text").innerText="Text changed!"}// Function to show an alert. function showAlert(){alert("Hello! This is an alert.")}// Function to add two numbers and print the result in the DOM. function sumNumbers(){var a=parseInt(document.getElementById("num1").value),b=parseInt(document.getElementById("num2").value);document.getElementById("result").innerText="The sum is: "+(a+b)}// Event to change the body background color. function changeBackgroundColor(){document.body.style.backgroundColor="#f0f0f0"}// Add events to buttons when the page loads. window.onload=function(){document.getElementById("change-text-btn").addEventListener("click",changeText),document.getElementById("alert-btn").addEventListener("click",showAlert),document.getElementById("sum-btn").addEventListener("click",sumNumbers),document.getElementById("change-bg-btn").addEventListener("click",changeBackgroundColor)}; This size is 1.09 KiB , which can be reduced much more by using plug-ins.   Essential Plug-ins. The use of plug-ins in Babel enhances the base package to the point of being unrecognizable. Some of the plug-ins I recommend are the following:  ➡ minify-replace  ➡ minify-simplify  ➡ minify-infinity  ➡ minify-builtins  ➡ minify-numeric-literals  ➡ minify-flip-comparisons  ➡ minify-constant-folding  ➡ minify-type-constructors  ➡ transform-minify-booleans  ➡ minify-guarded-expressions  ➡ transform-regexp-constructors  ➡ transform-merge-sibling-variables  ➡ transform-inline-consecutive-adds  ➡ transform-simplify-comparison-operators  ➡ babel-plugin-transform-remove-undefined  ➡ @babel/plugin-transform-member-expression-literals   Conclusion. The automatic compilation and optimization of JavaScript with Babel is an essential practice for improving web page performance. By significantly reducing file sizes, the file transfer rate is also reduced. This not only speeds up loading times but also maintains a high standard of quality and performance in projects and provides a smoother user experience across a variety of environments and devices.   /es/articulos/compilar-comprimir-y-mejorar-la-compatibilidad-de-los-archivos-javascript-con-babel /en/articles/compile-compress-and-improve-compatibility-javascript-files-babel

In the article Migrate Content Paragraphs with Migrate , I explore the possibilities of migrating Paragraphs in Drupal using migration configuration files that are independent of the parent node. However, although Paragraphs are an entity, they are not a primary entity and always depend on a parent. In this article, I show how to migrate Paragraphs and link them to the parent within the same migration, thus optimizing the migration process by reducing execution time, eliminating dependencies, and strengthening the parent-child relationship between the two entities, making this process a more convenient method than the one discussed in the previous article.   Dependencies. To use this method, it is necessary to install the module for Drupal : Migrate Child Entity Generate . You can install it from the “ Extend ” section of the Drupal administrator or with Composer : composer require drupal/migrate_child_entity_generate And enable it from the “ Extend ” section of the Drupal administrator or with Drush : drush en migrate_child_entity_generate   One Migrate plugin to rule them all. Using the child_entity_generate plugin from the Migrate Child Entity Generate module is very simple. You need to define the plugin, the entity type, the bundle type, and optionally define the variable and default constant values as in the following example: field_name: plugin: child_entity_generate entity_type: paragraph bundle: paragraph_bundle values: field_1: value_1 field_2/value: value_2 default_values: langcode: "en" field_2/format: "text" The difference between values and default_values is that in values , you introduce variable values for each different Paragraph (e.g., a text, a date, etc.), while in default_values , you introduce static and common values for all Paragraphs (e.g., the format of a CKEditor WYSIWYG field, a language selection field, etc.).   One Migrate plugin to rule all values. Unlike the entity_generate plugin from the Migrate Plus module, the child_entity_generate plugin does accept an array of values as a parameter, for example: destination: plugin: "entity:node" source: fields: - faq_items: - question: "Some question" answer: "Some answer" - question: "Another question" answer: "Another answer" process: field_faqs: plugin: child_entity_generate source: faq_items entity_type: field_collection bundle: faq values: field_faq_question: question field_faq_answer/value: answer default_values: field_faq_answer/format: "basic_html" The above code would create a faq_items entity of type faq for each item in the array faq_items , assigning the value of question to the field_faq_question field and the value of answer to the field_faq_answer field, with the basic_html format as the default value for the field_faq_answer field for all entities. It would then assign the target_id and target_revision_id of each entity to the field_faqs field.   ℹ️ As of the publication of this article, the Migrate Child Entity Generate module in the stable version 1.0.1 from June 4, 2024, does not accept references to fields from the current Row in the migration process (e.g., assigning "@other_field" to a field ). To fix this, I created a patch that the module maintainer accepted in the issue " Refine the process value filtering so that it gets values from the row ". If you need it, you can apply the following patch or install the development version 1.x-dev of the module.   Conclusion. Efficiently migrating Paragraphs in Drupal is a challenge, but using the Migrate Child Entity Generate module offers a powerful solution. Through this method, it is possible to integrate Paragraphs directly with their parent nodes in a single migration. Additionally, the child_entity_generate plugin provides a robust and effective method for migrating Paragraphs in Drupal .   /es/articulos/migrar-paragraphs-de-contenidos-con-migrate-version-mejorada /en/articles/migrate-paragraphs-content-migrate-enhanced-version

full: Selective entity update during Drupal migrations Drupal Migrate Publicado 25/08/2024 Lectura de 5 minutos Athlete jumping over hurdles Athlete jumping over hurdles Athlete jumping over hurdles When performing migrations in a system, it is sometimes necessary to update existing entities instead of creating new ones. However, this process can be complicated if only specific entities need to be modified. This article presents different approaches to facilitate the management of migrations according to the specific needs of each case. Sometimes, Drupal migrations need to update entities instead of creating them using the migration parameter --update . During this process, all entities from the previous migration will be updated, along with the possible creation of new entities. For better or worse, the new data will update all available entities in the system and data source. But what if it is necessary to update data for only some entities?   The unit method. If you need to update only a few entities, but not too many, you can add the --idlist parameter to the migration command, followed by the migration identifiers corresponding to each data group. For example, if you have the following data in JSON format: { "elements": [ { "element": { "id": "1", "name": "Name 1" }, "element": { "id": "2", "name": "Name 2" }, "element": { "id": "3", "name": "Name 3" }, "element": { "id": "4", "name": "Name 4" }, } ] } With this data injected into a migration, if you only need to migrate elements with id's 1 , 2 , and 3 , the parameter would be --idlist=1,2,3 . Applied to a full migration command with drush, it would look like this: drush migrate-import migrate_elements --idlist=1,2,3 If instead of creating them, you need to update them, the command would look like this with the --update parameter: drush migrate-import migrate_elements --update --idlist=1,2,3 This way of migrating individual entities is very simple and fast, but it is only applicable to a small number of identifiers (unless you feel like entering 1000 IDs into the command parameter, which a generative AI might handle well, but you'd have to see how the system supports it).     The collective method. Let's propose the following case: “ The editor needs you to migrate many, many, too many entities, a ton of entities. And this editor will individually check that all entities have been migrated correctly and would like to 'lock' somehow the entities that have been migrated correctly and update the data source for entities that were not migrated well. ” And you wonder if there is a way to update all entities except the locked ones. Well, the first thing would be to create a boolean field ( TRUE or FALSE ) that decides if an entity is locked or not, and now, the following custom Migrate plugin will check in the database if the entity in the current Row has already been migrated, and the value provided for the field provided in the field and value parameters of the plugin: /** * Migrate plugin that returns NULL if it finds the field next to the provided value or TRUE. * These return variables facilitate further processing such as skipping the row, for example. * It does not need a source and generates its own return value. * * @MigrateProcessPlugin( * id = "check_entity_field_value" * ) * * Example usage: * @code * check_entity_field_value_example: * plugin: check_entity_field_value * field: field_to_check * value: value_to_check * @endcode */ class CheckEntityFieldValue extends ProcessPluginBase implements ContainerFactoryPluginInterface { /** * The migration. * * @var \Drupal\migrate\Plugin\MigrationInterface|null */ protected $migration; /** * The entity type manager. * * @var \Drupal\Core\Entity\EntityTypeManagerInterface */ protected $entity_type_manager; /** * {@inheritdoc} */ public static function create(ContainerInterface $container, array $configuration, $plugin_id, $plugin_definition, MigrationInterface $migration = NULL) { $instance = new static($configuration, $plugin_id, $plugin_definition); $instance->entity_type_manager = $container->get('entity_type.manager'); $instance->migration = $migration; return $instance; } /** * {@inheritdoc} */ public function transform($value, MigrateExecutableInterface $migrate_executable, Row $row, $destination_property): bool|null { /** @var \Drupal\Core\Entity\EntityTypeInterface|string $entity_type */ $entity_type = $this->getMigrationTargetEntityType($this->migration); $field = (isset($this->configuration['field']) && is_string($this->configuration['field'])) ? $this->configuration['field'] : NULL; if (isset($entity_type) && isset($field)) { $destination_ids = $this->getEntityIdsFromRow($row); if (!empty($destination_ids)) { $value = (isset($this->configuration['value'])) ? $this->configuration['value'] : NULL; foreach ($destination_ids as $entity_id) { if (!$entity_id) { continue; } /** @var \Drupal\Core\Entity\EntityInterface|null $entity */ $entity = $this->entity_type_manager->getStorage($entity_type)->load($entity_id); if ($entity instanceof FieldableEntityInterface && $entity->hasField($field)) { // Returns NULL if it finds the field with any value // if the value is not specified, or if it is equal // to the value if the value has been specified. if ((isset($this->configuration['value']) && ((isset($entity->$field->value) && $entity->$field->value == $this->configuration['value']) || (isset($entity->$field->target_id) && $entity->target_id == $this->configuration['value']))) || (!isset($this->configuration['value']) && (isset($entity->$field->value) || isset($entity->$field->target_id)))) { return NULL; } } } } } return TRUE; } /** * Retrieves the target entity type for a given migration. * * @param \Drupal\migrate\Plugin\MigrationInterface $migration * The migration object from which to retrieve the target entity type. * * @return string|null * The target entity type if it can be determined. * * @throws \Exception $e */ protected function getMigrationTargetEntityType(MigrationInterface $migration): string|null { try { /** @var \Drupal\migrate\Plugin\MigrateDestinationInterface $migration_destination_plugin */ $migration_destination_plugin = $migration->getDestinationPlugin(); /** @var \Drupal\Component\Plugin\Definition\PluginDefinitionInterface|array $migration_destination_plugin_definition */ $migration_destination_plugin_definition = $migration_destination_plugin->getPluginDefinition(); // Gets from the plugin definition the id of the target entity, // it will always be the first match or none. preg_match('/:([^:]+)$/', $migration_destination_plugin_definition['id'], $entity_type); return (isset($entity_type[1]) && is_string($entity_type[1])) ? $entity_type[1] : NULL; } catch (\Exception $e) { return NULL; } } /** * Retrieves destination entity IDs from a migration row. * * @param \Drupal\migrate\Row $row * The migration row object from which to retrieve the entity IDs. * * @return array * An associative array of destination ID values. */ protected function getEntityIdsFromRow(Row $row): array { $destination_ids = []; $mid_map = $row->getIdMap(); if (!empty($mid_map)) { foreach ($mid_map as $mid_map_element => $mid_map_element_value) { // Destination IDs are always added with the same ID // and a counter (destid1, destid2, destid3, etc.). if (str_contains($mid_map_element, 'destid')) { $destination_ids[$mid_map_element] = $mid_map_element_value; } } } return $destination_ids; } } This plugin, for each Row , first gets the field parameter and the entity type to check using the getMigrationTargetEntityType() method with the current migration of the destination data using a regular expression. Then, it retrieves, if it exists, the destination entity with the getEntityIdsFromRow() method, which will need the current row to get raw data from the database; this result will only contain values if it is a migration update. Once this data is obtained, the destination entity can be loaded, and it can be checked if the field, if present, has the specified value.   Now you would need to add the plugin according to the example to the migration. For instance, if you need to skip the entity when the boolean field field_migrate_skip contains the value TRUE , the plugin will be defined as follows: skip_row_on_field_migrate_skip_true: - plugin: check_entity_field_value field: field_migrate_skip value: TRUE - plugin: skip_on_empty method: row message: 'Ignored because field field_migrate_skip is TRUE.' This will skip the Row of the migration if the value of the field_migrate_skip field is equal to TRUE because the plugin will return NULL , and the skip_on_empty plugin will identify it as an empty value. Otherwise, it will receive TRUE and will not skip the Row , leaving the entities “locked” by the editor intact. Although this is a fictional case, it has many applications, such as a mass update of entities by providing a field value if certain conditions are met.     Conclusion. Whether you need to update a few entities during a migration or skip just a few, there are different methods to perform this data update. It is only necessary to consider which method is most convenient for the migration's needs.   /es/articulos/actualizacion-selectiva-de-entidades-durante-migraciones-de-drupal /en/articles/selective-entity-update-during-drupal-migrations

Selective entity update during Drupal migrations

When performing migrations in a system, it is sometimes necessary to update existing entities instead of creating new ones. However, this process can be complicated if only specific entities need to be modified. This article presents different approaches to facilitate the management of migrations according to the specific needs of each case.
